title: The Bell Does Not Lie
brief: Alderman Cornelius Reeve went into the library at the Delgado Assembly Rooms during a subscription dinner and did not come out. Nine people were in the building and every one of them can tell you exactly where they stood when the Bell of Order struck nine, because that is the sort of evening it was. All nine accounts agree. That is the first thing about this case that ought to worry you.

suspects.name: Cassian Vole
suspects.summary: Twelve years at Reeve's elbow, on a clerk's wage, never once late. Winds the Assembly Rooms clocks on a Tuesday as an unpaid courtesy, which everybody knows and nobody has ever thought about.
suspects.alibi: At the long table from just after the bell. Four people will swear to it, and all four are telling the truth.

suspects.name: Hesper Lyne
suspects.summary: Wanted Reeve's committee chair and made no secret of it. Wrote him a letter last month that the recipient described to three people as a threat.
suspects.alibi: On the terrace with a cigar when the bell went. The steward saw her go out and saw her come back.

suspects.name: Dr. Ambrose Teague
suspects.summary: Certified the death on the spot and wrote a time on the certificate without consulting anything but his own watch.
suspects.alibi: In the card room. Three players, two of whom were paying attention.

suspects.name: Lady Ottilie Marchmont
suspects.summary: Found the body. Owed Reeve four hundred pounds against a house she has not lived in for six years.
suspects.alibi: Circulating, in front of everybody, until she opened the library door and screamed.

suspects.name: Rufus Kell
suspects.summary: Last man to see Reeve alive. Was to be dismissed at the end of the quarter over a discrepancy in the cellar book.
suspects.alibi: On the door, where a steward is. Everybody walked past him all evening.

motives.label: To bury a sold vote
motives.description: Committee decisions are worth money to a man who knows them a day early, and worth a great deal more to the man who does not want it known he was selling them.

motives.label: The chair
motives.description: Reeve held a committee chair that another alderman wanted badly enough to write about.

motives.label: A debt called in
motives.description: Four hundred pounds and a house, and Reeve had stopped being patient about both.

motives.label: To keep a position
motives.description: A man dismissed without a character at fifty does not find another post in this city.

clues.title: Reeve, in the library
clues.body: Face down between the reading desk and the fire, one blow to the back of the head, no defensive marks. He was struck by somebody he did not think worth turning round for.

clues.title: The brass lamp
clues.body: Back on its table, upright, and wiped. Somebody took the trouble — which is more thought than most killers manage in the first ten minutes.

clues.title: Laboratory report on the lamp
clues.body: The brass is clean. The felt on the underside is not: there is candle wax there, and set into the wax a partial impression of a hand. It is a small hand, and it took hold of the lamp by the base, upside down, the way you would pick up something you meant to swing.

clues.title: The last man to see him
clues.body: Kell put Reeve into the library himself, with a decanter, a few minutes before the Bell of Order struck nine. Reeve said he was expecting somebody and did not say who.

clues.title: When she opened the door
clues.body: Lady Marchmont went to fetch Reeve for the toast about twenty minutes after the bell. She is precise about it because she had been counting down to the toast all evening.

clues.title: The coroner's own estimate
clues.body:
The coroner has read Dr. Teague's certificate and does not think much of it. On temperature and stiffening he puts death at a quarter to nine, give or take ten minutes — and he will say so under oath.

Which cannot be. Reeve was walked into that library alive a few minutes BEFORE the bell struck nine, and eight people will swear to the bell.

clues.title: A folded card in the striking train
clues.body:
Wedged into the striking train of the Bell of Order, worn soft by two hundred strikes: a subscription card for the Delgado Assembly Rooms, folded four times.

The jam does not stop the bell. It releases the train early. On the night Reeve died, the Bell of Order struck nine at eight forty-one — and nine people built their evening on it.

clues.title: The winding book
clues.body:
The Assembly Rooms clocks and the Bell of Order are on one contract, and the contract has not been paid in two years — because a gentleman does it as a courtesy. Every Tuesday, initialled in the same small hand: C.V.

He wound it on the Tuesday. Reeve died on the Thursday.

clues.title: The committee minute book
clues.body: Four contracts in eighteen months, each awarded to a bidder who revised their figure two days before the vote, each revision landing within a shilling of the winning margin. The minutes are taken and copied in the secretary's hand.

clues.title: A clerk's bank book
clues.body: Cash paid in on four occasions in eighteen months, each within a week of a committee award, none of them under sixty pounds. A secretary's wage is a hundred and ten a year.

clues.title: An unsent letter
clues.body: In Reeve's hand, undated, in his own desk. It begins: I have gone back over the Hollis award and the Draycott award and I do not care for what I find, and I care still less that the hand it is written in is one I trained. It ends mid-sentence.

clues.title: Lyne's letter
clues.body: You have held that chair four years on a majority of one and you will not hold it five. Signed, and dated last month. She does not deny writing it and does not appear to think she should.

clues.title: The doctor's case
clues.body: Morphine, and rather more of it than a club physician's duties would account for, and a prescription pad made out to four names that do not appear in any directory.

clues.title: A demand, politely worded
clues.body: Reeve to Lady Marchmont, a fortnight ago: I have carried this since the spring and I am afraid I have carried it as far as I intend to. Four hundred pounds against a house in Harrowfield she cannot afford to lose twice.

clues.title: The cellar book
clues.body: Eleven bottles short across the quarter, entered and initialled by the steward. Reeve chaired the house committee that was to hear it. Kell would have been out without a character by Michaelmas.

clues.title: The secretary's account
clues.body: He took his seat at the long table just after the bell and did not leave it. Four people confirm this without hesitation, and they are not lying. He is very calm about it, and he tells it the same way twice, which most people do not.

clues.title: Lyne, on the terrace
clues.body: "I wanted his chair and I would have taken it off him at the vote in March, in public, which is the only way worth taking anything." She does not soften it. "Killing him gets me a by-election and a rival with a martyr's obituary. Use your head."

clues.title: The death certificate
clues.body: Time of death entered as twenty past nine, in Teague's hand, signed on the spot. He arrived at the body eight minutes after Lady Marchmont screamed and wrote down the time he was told the bell had struck, plus twenty.

questions.text: When did you last see Alderman Reeve?
questions.answer: "Walked him in myself with the decanter. Few minutes before the bell — I know because I was watching the clock for the toast." He does not blink. "Said he was expecting someone. Didn't say who, and I don't ask."

questions.text: You were to be dismissed at the quarter.
questions.answer: "Eleven bottles. Over three months, in a house that drinks four hundred." He straightens a chair that does not need it. "I entered it myself, in the book, in my own hand. A man covering himself does not write it down."

questions.text: Take me to when you opened the door.
questions.answer: "Twenty minutes after the bell. I had been counting down to the toast since eight — you do, when it is your evening." Her hands are perfectly still, which is its own kind of tell. "I opened the door and he was on the floor and I am afraid I was no use at all."

questions.text: You owed him four hundred pounds.
questions.answer: "I owe a great many people a great many things. Cornelius was the only one who never once mentioned it in a room with anybody else in it." She looks up. "You will find that people who are being blackmailed do not usually host dinners for the blackmailer."

questions.text: Dr. Teague put the time at twenty past nine.
questions.answer:
"Dr. Teague put the time at twenty past nine because somebody told him the bell had struck at nine." She does not look up from the sheet. "On temperature and stiffening this man died at a quarter to. Ten minutes either side and I will still say a quarter to, and I will say it in a witness box."

Which is a problem, because eight people watched him walk into that library alive AFTER a quarter to nine.

"I took my seat at the long table just after the bell and I did not leave it until Lady Marchmont screamed." He offers you tea. "Mr. Kell will confirm it, and Mrs. Alderton, and the Draycotts. I am sorry to be so dull about it."

The teacup goes down without a sound. "I wind them because nobody else will pay to. Twelve years I have done small unpaid things for that man and this is the first time anybody has asked me about one."

He does not ask which clock.

questions.text: Four contracts, four revisions, four deposits.
questions.answer:
"He trained me." A long pause; he is not performing it. "Twelve years at a hundred and ten a year and he could not see why I might want more. He found the Hollis award on the Tuesday and told me he would give me until the Thursday to explain myself."

He stops there. He is far too careful to finish the sentence.

"I wrote it, I meant it, and I would write it again." She does not put the papers down. "I wanted his chair and I would have had it off him in March at the vote, in front of the whole council. Killing him gets me a by-election and an opponent nobody is allowed to criticise. Use your head."

questions.text: How did you arrive at twenty past nine?
questions.answer:
"The bell had gone nine. Lady Marchmont found him twenty minutes after. I was fetched, I attended, I wrote it down." He is already reaching for his hat. "That is not an estimate, it is arithmetic."

It is arithmetic. It is arithmetic built entirely on the bell.

locations.description: Two rooms above a tobacconist. The council's letter of engagement is on the desk, which means for once somebody respectable is paying, and for once you do not entirely trust the reason.
Delgado Assembly Rooms. Long table, card room, terrace, and a library at the back with one door and a fire that had burned down by the time anybody thought to look at it.
Cast in a year nobody agrees on, and the only clock in Marrowgate that everybody trusts without checking. The striking train is behind a door that has not been locked in living memory.
Tile, drains, and a cold that gets into your coat. Dr. Sokolov has read the club physician's certificate twice and has opinions about it.
Granite steps and a committee room where four contracts were awarded in eighteen months. The minute books are public, which is the sort of thing nobody remembers until somebody asks.
The Grand Crown Apartments. Cassian Vole keeps three rooms, very clean, with a shelf of Reeve's old speeches bound at his own expense.
Voss & Delgado, Attorneys. Reeve's solicitors, and the only people in Marrowgate who kept copies of his correspondence when he did not.
Chapel of the Crimson Sparrow. Lady Marchmont has been here every morning since, which the verger finds admirable and you find worth a question.
Where the city decides what happened. Alderman Lyne is in the gallery most days, taking notes on people who will one day need her.
The Crimson Dial. Half the council drinks here and all of it talks. The steward's cellar book trouble was common knowledge a month before the committee heard of it.
Six floors of filing. The Reeve file is thin, closed, and initialled by somebody who did not want it opened again.
The northern line's last stop, two streets from the Assembly Rooms. Half the dinner arrived through it and every one of them set their watch by the bell on the way past.

solution.epilogue:
The evening was never wrong. The clock was.

Cassian Vole wound the Bell of Order on the Tuesday, as he had every Tuesday for two years without being paid or thanked, and he left a folded subscription card in the striking train. It does not stop a bell. It releases it early. On the Thursday the Bell of Order struck nine at eight forty-one, and nine people at a subscription dinner built the entire evening on it — including the four who gave him his alibi, who were telling the exact truth and had no idea what they were telling it about.

Reeve went into the library at a few minutes before the bell, which everyone understood as a few minutes before nine and which was in fact around half past eight. Vole followed him in, took up the lamp by its base the way you pick up a thing you mean to swing, and was at the long table by ten to. Everyone remembers him arriving just after the bell. Everyone is right. Just after the bell was eight forty-one.

The coroner never budged. A quarter to nine, she said, and ten minutes either side, and she said it in the witness box exactly as she promised. The defence spent two days trying to move her and moved her by nothing at all.

He is convicted on the winding book. Twelve years of small unpaid courtesies, and the last of them hanged him.
solution.failureEpilogue:
The Assizes hear a great deal about a letter, a cellar book, and four hundred pounds owed against a house in Harrowfield, and rather less about a folded subscription card that nobody thought to look for. The Bell of Order is serviced in the spring by a firm that is actually paid for it, and the card comes out of the striking train and goes into a bin, and the bell keeps better time thereafter, and nobody remarks on it.

Cassian Vole gives evidence for the prosecution. He is described in two newspapers as the dead man's most loyal servant, and he weeps in the box, and it is not entirely an act — he did admire him. He takes a post with the Ravensgate ward in the autumn and winds their clocks too, as a courtesy, because nobody else will pay to.

keyPoints.claim: The coroner puts death at about a quarter to nine, which is nowhere near the time the Bell of Order appeared to give.
The bell was jammed with a folded subscription card so that it struck the wrong hour, and the alibi everyone accepted was built on that wrong hour.
Vole maintained the Assembly Rooms clocks and the Bell of Order on one unpaid contract, which is how he could reach the striking train at all - and he was burying a committee vote he had sold.
